transcript.text: hob keeps making a noise after i turn it off

What this is depends mostly on the type of hob and the sound it makes. 1. A cooling fan running on (induction hobs). This is normal. Induction hobs have a fan under the glass that cools the electronics, and it often carries on whirring for a few minutes after you switch off, sometimes up to 10 or 15 minutes after a long or hot cook, then stops by itself. It's only a concern if it never stops, makes a grinding or rattling sound, or comes with a burning smell or an error code.
2. Rapid clicking from a gas hob. That's the spark igniter firing when it shouldn't. Usually a burner cap or the igniter tip is wet (often after cleaning or a boil-over) or greasy. Less often a knob's ignition switch is sticking.
3. Ticking or creaking as a ceramic or solid-plate hob cools. That's normal too: the glass, metal and frame contract as they cool, and it fades within a few minutes. 1. Listen to where the sound comes from and what it's like. A steady whirr or hum from underneath points to the fan. A fast tick-tick-tick, perhaps with a visible spark at a burner, means the igniter. 2. Time it. If it stops on its own within about 15 minutes, a fan or cooling noise is probably normal. If it carries on indefinitely, it's a fault.
3. If it's gas and clicking: make sure every knob is fully back in the off position. Let the hob go cold, then lift off the burner caps and crowns. Clean and fully dry them, gently wipe the white igniter tips, and re-seat the caps so they sit flat. If it was wet or dirty, the clicking often stops once it's dry. Leave it a few hours if it's been soaked. If a gas hob still clicks with all knobs off and everything dry, the ignition switch or module is the likely cause, and that's a job for a Gas Safe engineer rather than something to take apart yourself. If you ever smell gas, turn it off at the supply, ventilate the room and call the gas emergency line. What type of hob is it, and what does the noise sound like?

its a Neff induction one, the black glass kind. a steady whirr from underneath, same as when im cooking. it stops by itself after 5 to 10 minutes. no smell and no error codes. im worried it might catch fire though

No, this isn't a fire risk. What you're describing is the hob doing exactly what it's designed to do. Under the glass, an induction hob has electronics that get warm while you cook, and a fan cools them. Most hobs, Neff included, keep that fan running after you switch off until the electronics have cooled, then stop it automatically. A steady whirr from underneath, the same sound you hear while cooking, that stops on its own after 5 to 10 minutes, with no smell and no error codes, is the classic normal pattern. The fan is there to protect the electronics, and if anything ever did get too hot, the hob would cut the power and show a code rather than carry on. It's worth keeping the hob able to breathe so the fan doesn't have to work harder than it needs to:
1. Check the space directly under the hob. If it's above a drawer, don't pack it right up to the underside, and keep tea towels, foil and paper away from it.
2. If there's a vent slot at the back edge of the hob or along the worktop, keep it clear of crumbs and clutter. It would become a fault worth looking at if:
• the fan never stops, or starts running much longer than it does now
• it grinds, rattles or screeches
• you get a burning or hot-plastic smell
• the hob switches off mid-cook or shows an error code If you smell burning, switch the hob off at its wall isolator or the consumer unit, stop using it, and get an engineer to look at it. As things stand, though, you don't need to do anything.
